title: Triton and tile-based GPU programming
why: Triton is the code TorchInductor generates for GPUs, and Liger Kernel and many FlashAttention variants are written in it. You program tiles, not threads. You already wrote a CUDA codegen backend; now add a Triton one.

steps.title: Tillet, Kung, Cox: Triton: An Intermediate Language and Compiler for Tiled Neural Network Computations (MAPL 2019)
steps.detail: Sections 3-5: Triton-C, Triton-IR, and Triton-JIT (tile-level passes and the auto-tuner in 5.3). Compare Triton-IR with your own IR.

steps.title: Triton tutorial 01: Vector Addition
steps.detail: program_id, masks, BLOCK_SIZE as tl.constexpr; run the benchmark and plot GB/s vs. size.

steps.title: Triton tutorial 02: Fused Softmax
steps.detail: One row per program. The tutorial's plot shows Triton about 4x faster than the unfused Torch JIT version; reproduce that comparison on your GPU.

steps.title: Triton tutorial 03: Matrix Multiplication
steps.detail: Block tiling, program re-ordering for L2 hit rate (GROUP_SIZE_M), autotune configs. The tutorial claims fp16 performance on par with cuBLAS; measure your ratio at 4096^2.

steps.title: Triton tutorial 04: Low-Memory Dropout
steps.detail: Seeded dropout using Triton's Philox-based RNG: regenerate the mask from a seed instead of storing it.

steps.title: Triton tutorial 05: Layer Normalization
steps.detail: Forward and backward. The hard part is the backward's two-stage parallel reduction of dW/db using Lock/Count and tl.atomic_cas.

steps.title: Triton tutorial 06: Fused Attention
steps.detail: The tutorial implements the FlashAttention-2 algorithm. Read it alongside the FA2 paper below.

steps.title: Triton-Puzzles (Sasha Rush)
steps.detail: 12 puzzles, from Constant Add to Simple FlashAttention (9), 2D convolution (10), matmul (11) and quantized matmul (12). They run in the Triton interpreter, no GPU needed.

steps.title: FlashAttention (Dao et al. 2022)
steps.detail: Sections 2-3: tiling and recomputation (3.1), IO-complexity analysis (3.2). Derive the HBM-access bound yourself.

steps.title: FlashAttention-2
steps.detail: Section 3: algorithm (3.1), parallelism over sequence length (3.2), work partitioning between warps (3.3).

steps.title: Horace He, Making Deep Learning Go Brrrr
steps.detail: Classify each kernel you benchmark as compute-, memory- or overhead-bound.

steps.title: Port one of your compiler's kernels to a Triton backend
steps.detail: Add a Triton codegen target for elementwise+reduce fusions; diff outputs against your CUDA backend.

build: A Triton backend for your compiler (elementwise and reduction codegen) plus the six tutorials reproduced with benchmark plots.
check: Tutorial 03 matmul reaches >=80% of torch.matmul (cuBLAS) fp16 TFLOPS at 4096^2 on your GPU
Fused attention matches torch SDPA to 1e-2 (fp16) for causal and non-causal
Your compiler emits Triton for a fused LayerNorm and it passes your test suite
You can explain grouped program ordering and why it raises L2 hit rate
outcomes: Write and autotune Triton kernels for matmul, reductions and attention.
Generate Triton from your own compiler IR.
stuck: Wrong results only at odd sizes: you forgot a mask on load or store; test sizes like 1000 and 4097, not just powers of two
Autotune 'wins' that vanish: you benchmarked with a cold cache or included compilation; use triton.testing.do_bench
Layernorm backward races: re-read the lock/atomic section of tutorial 05 before inventing your own reduction
Attention numerically off: check you rescale the running accumulator when the running max changes (FA2 paper, Algorithm 1)
Puzzles confusing: print shapes with the interpreter mode (TRITON_INTERPRET=1) on CPU

project.title: Fused kernel library: beat torch.compile on three real ops
project.brief: In nanoGPT (GPT-2 124M config, block size 1024) write Triton forward and backward kernels for RMSNorm+residual, SwiGLU, and fused linear cross-entropy over the 50,257-token vocab. Autotune them, swap them into the model, and report training step time and peak memory against eager PyTorch and torch.compile.
deliverables: repo with kernels, gradcheck tests and a pip-installable package
README with roofline plots (achieved GB/s or TFLOPS vs. peak) across sizes
a 600–1200 word write-up explaining each fusion, the bound it hits and what limited further gains

rubric.solid: All three kernels pass gradcheck; each is >=1.3x eager and within 10% of torch.compile; roofline plot per kernel
rubric.exceptional: At least one kernel beats torch.compile by >=1.2x end to end, e.g. a chunked fused cross-entropy that cuts peak memory by >2x, with Nsight Compute evidence for why

references.title: Liger Kernel (fused Triton kernels for LLM training)

title: CUTLASS, CuTe and Hopper/Blackwell features
why: The fastest H100/B200 kernels (FlashAttention-3, cuBLAS-class GEMMs) use TMA, wgmma and warp specialization. CUTLASS and its CuTe layout library expose these directly; Triton exposes them only partly.

steps.title: Simon Boehm, How to Optimize a CUDA Matmul Kernel
steps.detail: Warm-up: the article covers kernels 1-6, 9 (autotuning) and 10 (warptiling); it skips 7 and 8 in the text. Re-derive them for the vocabulary used below.

steps.title: CuTe quickstart (CUTLASS docs)
steps.detail: Then read 01_layout.md, 02_layout_algebra.md, 03_tensor.md and 0x_gemm_tutorial.md in the same folder; 0z_tma_tensors.md before the Hopper GEMM.

steps.title: CuTe docs folder: layout algebra exercises
steps.detail: Hand-compute composition, complement and logical_divide on 2-3 layouts; check with cute::print.

steps.title: Colfax: CUTLASS Tutorial: Efficient GEMM kernel designs with Pipelining
steps.detail: Software pipelining of the mainloop with mbarriers, and warp-specialized producer/consumer designs.

steps.title: Colfax: CUTLASS Tutorial: Mastering the NVIDIA Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA)
steps.detail: TMA load and store, TMA store reduce, TMA load multicast, and the PTX they map to.

steps.title: Colfax: CUTLASS Tutorial: Fast Matrix-Multiplication with WGMMA on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs
steps.detail: Warpgroup MMA, smem layout requirements, and wgmma.fence / commit_group / wait_group (cute::warpgroup_arrive, commit_batch, wait).

steps.title: PTX ISA: wgmma and cp.async.bulk sections
steps.detail: Look up wgmma.mma_async and cp.async.bulk.tensor; see exactly what CuTe emits.

steps.title: FlashAttention-3
steps.detail: Section 3.1: producer-consumer warp specialization and pingpong scheduling; 3.2: overlapping GEMM and softmax inside a warpgroup; 3.3: FP8, including incoherent processing.

steps.title: ThunderKittens: Simple, Fast, and Adorable AI Kernels
steps.detail: Tile primitives between Triton and CUTLASS in abstraction level. Compare with what you wrote in module 32.

steps.title: ThunderKittens: run the educational H100 GEMM series
steps.detail: Build kernels/gemm/educational_h100 step by step; profile each step with Nsight Compute and name what changed.

steps.title: Write a Hopper GEMM in CuTe
steps.detail: TMA load -> smem -> wgmma, 2-4 stage pipeline, then add warp specialization. No GPU with sm90? Rent one by the hour.

build: A from-scratch CuTe GEMM for H100 progressing from SIMT to wgmma+TMA+warp-specialized, each step benchmarked.
check: Final GEMM reaches >=70% of cuBLAS bf16 at 8192^2 on H100
You can draw the CuTe layout (shape:stride) of an smem tile with swizzle
You can explain why warp specialization helps when TMA is async
Nsight Compute report shows tensor-core utilization per version
outcomes: Compute CuTe layout composition and logical_divide by hand and check with cute::print.
Build a TMA+wgmma pipelined GEMM on Hopper and measure it against cuBLAS.
stuck: Template error walls: compile tiny examples first and use cute::print/print_latex to inspect layouts
wgmma hangs or garbage: missing fence/commit/wait or wrong smem swizzle; compare with the Colfax wgmma post line by line
No Hopper GPU: do the layout and SIMT parts locally, then rent an H100 for a few hours with a script ready
TMA descriptor errors: global tensor must be 16-byte aligned and strides multiples of 16 bytes
Lost in CUTLASS 3 collectives: read the Colfax pipelining post before the source

project.title: bf16 MoE grouped GEMM on Hopper with a public benchmark
project.brief: Implement a warp-specialized Hopper grouped GEMM for MoE layers in bf16, using the expert shapes from Mixtral 8x7B (hidden 4096, FFN 14336, 8 experts, top-2) at token counts 128, 512 and 4096. Benchmark against a loop of cuBLAS GEMMs and document each optimization with Nsight Compute evidence.
deliverables: repo with the kernel, a PyTorch extension binding and correctness tests
README with TFLOPS tables vs. baselines across >=6 shapes
a 600–1200 word write-up walking through the pipeline, layouts and the remaining gap

rubric.solid: >=60% of the best public baseline on all shapes, correct to fp tolerance, profiler screenshots
rubric.exceptional: Beats the cuBLAS loop on small token counts and explains why with occupancy and pipeline analysis.

title: Industrial ML compilers: MLIR, XLA/StableHLO, TorchInductor, TVM
why: XLA, TorchInductor, TVM and MLIR-based stacks are what production ML compilers look like. You built a toy compiler; here you read how these systems split IR levels, fusion and codegen, and you build a small dialect in MLIR.

steps.title: MLIR: A Compiler Infrastructure for the End of Moore's Law (Lattner et al.)
steps.detail: Sections 2-4: design principles, IR design (ops, regions, dialects), and the pass/rewrite infrastructure.

steps.title: j2kun mlir-tutorial: Getting started
steps.detail: Build mlir-opt from the tutorial repo with Bazel (CMake also described). The first LLVM build takes hours; start it early.

steps.title: j2kun: Running and testing a lowering
steps.detail: Write lit tests with FileCheck; every later step in this module is tested this way.

steps.title: j2kun: Writing our first pass
steps.detail: An affine loop-unroll pass, then the same transform as a rewrite pattern.

steps.title: j2kun: Defining a new dialect
steps.detail: Define the tutorial's poly (polynomial) dialect with TableGen ops and types.

steps.title: j2kun: Canonicalizers and declarative rewrite patterns
steps.detail: Canonicalization patterns in C++ and in DRR (TableGen) for the poly dialect.

steps.title: j2kun: Dialect conversion
steps.detail: TypeConverter and ConversionTarget: lower the poly dialect to standard upstream dialects.

steps.title: j2kun: Lowering through LLVM
steps.detail: Lower to the LLVM dialect, translate with mlir-translate, and link the result into an executable.

steps.title: OpenXLA: XLA architecture
steps.detail: How XLA takes StableHLO, runs target-independent passes (CSE, fusion, buffer analysis), converts to HLO and hands off to a backend for target-specific fusion and codegen.

steps.title: TorchInductor: a PyTorch-native Compiler with Define-by-Run IR and Symbolic Shapes (Jason Ansel, 2022)
steps.detail: Define-by-run loop IR, scheduling and fusion, Triton codegen for GPUs.

steps.title: PyTorch 2: Faster Machine Learning Through Dynamic Python Bytecode Transformation and Graph Compilation (ASPLOS 2024)
steps.detail: Section 3 TorchDynamo (bytecode capture, guards, graph breaks), Section 4 TorchInductor, Section 5 dynamic shapes.

steps.title: TVM: An Automated End-to-End Optimizing Compiler for Deep Learning (OSDI 2018)
steps.detail: Section 3 graph-level fusion, Section 4 tensor expressions and schedules, Section 5 the ML-based cost model.

build: A toy 'tg' MLIR dialect (add, mul, matmul, reduce) with canonicalization patterns and a lowering to linalg, then loops, then LLVM, tested with lit and FileCheck.
check: The lowered tg matmul, compiled to a binary, matches a numpy matmul on random 64x64 inputs
At least 10 FileCheck tests cover canonicalization and each lowering stage
A one-page table comparing your compiler, XLA, Inductor and TVM on IR levels, fusion, scheduling and autotuning, with a source citation per cell
You can dump Inductor's generated Triton for a two-layer MLP (TORCH_LOGS=output_code) and point to each fused kernel
outcomes: Define an MLIR dialect in TableGen, write canonicalization and conversion passes, and lower it to LLVM
Read XLA HLO dumps and Inductor output and say which ops were fused into which kernel
Name, for XLA, Inductor and TVM, where fusion and scheduling decisions are made
stuck: Build too slow: build LLVM once in release mode with ccache, at the commit the tutorial pins
TableGen errors: start from the tutorial's poly dialect and change one thing at a time
'failed to legalize operation': check which ops the ConversionTarget marks legal and that the TypeConverter handles block arguments
Inductor output too long: start with a two-op function and TORCH_LOGS=output_code,schedule

project.title: Lower your course compiler's IR through MLIR
project.brief: Make your course compiler emit the tg dialect, reuse upstream linalg tiling and fusion, and run a 3-layer MLP (784-256-256-10, fp32, batch 64) on CPU through MLIR. Compare runtime with your hand-written backend and with torch.compile on the same machine. Alternative: measure TorchInductor fusion decisions (kernel count and runtime) on 5 HuggingFace models, including GPT-2 small and BERT-base, and write a minimal patch that improves one case.
deliverables: repo with the dialect, passes, FileCheck tests and an end-to-end example
README with performance comparison vs. your original backend and vs. torch.compile
a 600–1200 word write-up on what MLIR made easier or harder than your own IR

rubric.solid: The MLP runs end to end through MLIR and matches PyTorch outputs to 1e-5; 20+ lit tests
rubric.exceptional: The MLP or a single transformer block runs on GPU via the MLIR GPU dialect within 2x of torch.compile, or the Inductor patch is opened upstream with benchmarks

title: Scheduling theory: polyhedral model and auto-schedulers
why: Your BEAM search picked schedules by trial. Two other approaches exist: polyhedral compilers prove which transforms are legal from dependences, and learned auto-schedulers predict runtime with a cost model. This module covers both.

steps.title: Halide: A Language and Compiler for Optimizing Parallelism, Locality, and Recomputation (PLDI 2013)
steps.detail: The algorithm/schedule split and the tradeoff between locality, parallelism and redundant recomputation.

steps.title: Learning to Optimize Halide with Tree Search and Random Programs (SIGGRAPH 2019)
steps.detail: Beam search over a large schedule space with a cost model trained on random programs; compare with your BEAM.

steps.title: Ansor: Generating High-Performance Tensor Programs for Deep Learning (OSDI 2020)
steps.detail: Section 4 program sampling (sketch generation, random annotation), Section 5 evolutionary fine-tuning with a learned cost model, Section 6 the task scheduler.

steps.title: Presburger Formulas and Polyhedral Compilation (Verdoolaege, isl tutorial)
steps.detail: Chapters 2-3 (sets, relations), Chapter 5 (instance sets, access relations, dependences, schedules) and Chapter 6 (dependence analysis). Run the examples with isl's Python interface or islpy.

steps.title: Pluto: polyhedral source-to-source
steps.detail: Run Pluto on a 2D stencil and a matmul and read the tiling hyperplanes it reports.

steps.title: Tiramisu: A Polyhedral Compiler for Expressing Fast and Portable Code (CGO 2019)
steps.detail: A Halide-like scheduling language built on a polyhedral representation.

steps.title: Dependence analysis in your compiler
steps.detail: Using islpy, compute dependences for your loop IR and reject tile or interchange transforms that violate them.

steps.title: Learned cost model for your BEAM search
steps.detail: Collect (schedule features, measured runtime) pairs, train a gradient-boosted tree, and use its ranking to prune BEAM candidates before measuring.

build: islpy-based legality checks for your loop transforms, and a learned cost model that reduces how many schedules BEAM has to measure.
check: Your compiler rejects interchanging the loops of a[i][j] = a[i-1][j+1] and accepts interchange on a matmul
Cost-model-guided search reaches within 10% of plain BEAM's best runtime using at most 25% of its measurements, on 5 kernels
You can write the iteration domain and the tiled schedule of a matmul as isl sets and maps
A one-page comparison of the Halide 2019 autoscheduler, Ansor and Pluto: search space, cost model, legality handling
outcomes: Write loop nests as isl sets and maps and check transform legality from dependences
Train and evaluate a learned cost model for schedule search, split by program
stuck: isl notation unfamiliar: write each tutorial example by hand first, then check it with isl
Cost model looks too good: split train/test by program, not by schedule, or schedules of the same program leak
Measurements noisy: lock GPU clocks, warm up, take the median of repeated runs
Pluto fails to build: use a container; the tiling hyperplanes are what you need from it

project.title: Reproduce a cost-model result on your own compiler
project.brief: Reproduce the core claim of the Halide 2019 autoscheduler, Ansor or TenSet inside your compiler: a learned cost model makes search more sample-efficient. Use their feature ideas on your search space, measure on at least 10 matmul/conv/reduction shapes, and report sample-efficiency curves and transfer from one GPU to another or from one op type to another.
deliverables: repo with the dataset of measured schedules (released), training code and integration
README with search-time vs. achieved-performance curves against random and plain BEAM
a 600–1200 word write-up on what transferred, what didn't and why

rubric.solid: Dataset of >=20k measured schedules, cost model with reported rank correlation, clear sample-efficiency plot
rubric.exceptional: Shows cross-hardware transfer or a novel feature that measurably helps; written like a workshop paper

references.title: TenSet (NeurIPS 2021 Datasets and Benchmarks), code and dataset

title: Numerics and low precision
why: LLM decoding is limited by memory bandwidth, so serving stacks store weights and activations in fp8, int4 or MX formats. This module covers how these formats lose precision and how GPTQ, AWQ and SmoothQuant recover it.

steps.title: Fabien Sanglard, Floating point visually explained
steps.detail: Warm-up. Then derive by hand the max value, min normal and epsilon of bf16, fp16, fp8 E4M3 and E5M2.

steps.title: FP8 Formats for Deep Learning (Micikevicius et al.)
steps.detail: Section 3: E4M3 vs E5M2 encodings, special values (E4M3 has no infinity) and exponent bias. Section 4: training and inference results and per-tensor scaling.

steps.title: OCP Microscaling (MX) Formats v1.0 spec
steps.detail: Section 5: MX block structure, element types (MXFP8, MXFP6, MXFP4, MXINT8) and the E8M0 shared scale. Section 6: dot products and conversion from fp32 vectors.

steps.title: Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning
steps.detail: Training and inference results with MX formats.

steps.title: LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale
steps.detail: Outlier feature dimensions and the mixed-precision decomposition that keeps them in fp16.

steps.title: SmoothQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for LLMs
steps.detail: Moving activation outliers into weights with per-channel scales; derive the migration strength alpha.

steps.title: GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers
steps.detail: Section 3 (layer-wise quantization, OBQ) and Section 4 (the GPTQ algorithm: arbitrary order, lazy batch updates, Cholesky reformulation).

steps.title: AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration
steps.detail: Per-channel scaling chosen from activation magnitudes; compare its assumptions with GPTQ.

steps.title: FP8 training recipe in Transformer Engine
steps.detail: Read the FP8 section of the user guide and the delayed-scaling recipe (amax history, scale update); run the FP8 example on a small model.

steps.title: Bit-exact format emulators
steps.detail: numpy emulators for bf16, fp8 E4M3/E5M2 and MXFP4 with round-to-nearest-even and saturation, tested against torch.float8_e4m3fn and torch.float8_e5m2.

steps.title: Quantized matmul kernel
steps.detail: W4A16 Triton kernel that loads packed int4 weights and dequantizes in registers; add it to your compiler as a dtype.

build: Format emulators, GPTQ and AWQ written from scratch and applied to a 1-2B model (for example Llama-3.2-1B or Qwen2.5-1.5B), and a W4A16 kernel used by your compiler.
check: Emulators bit-match torch.float8_e4m3fn and torch.float8_e5m2 casts on 1e6 random fp32 values, including subnormals and out-of-range values
Your 4-bit GPTQ model (group size 128) is within 0.5 WikiText-2 perplexity of a reference GPTQ implementation at the same context length
Your W4A16 kernel beats the fp16 matmul at batch size 1 on the model's MLP shapes
You can explain why E4M3 has no infinity and what that means for scale selection
outcomes: Derive and emulate fp8 and MX formats bit-exactly
Implement GPTQ and AWQ and locate which layers cause accuracy loss
Write a fused dequantize-matmul kernel and measure it against fp16
stuck: Emulator off by one ulp: you truncated instead of rounding to nearest even, or mishandled subnormals
GPTQ diverges: add dampening to the Hessian diagonal; the paper uses 1% of the average diagonal value
Perplexity differs from papers: match context length, dataset split and tokenizer
Quantized kernel slow: dequantize in registers after loading packed ints, not into shared memory

project.title: Precision study: how low can a real LLM go?
project.brief: Take Llama-3.2-1B or Qwen2.5-1.5B and evaluate bf16, fp8 (per-tensor vs. per-channel), MXFP8, MXFP4 (emulated) and int4 (GPTQ vs. AWQ). Measure WikiText-2 perplexity, accuracy on one downstream task (for example HellaSwag via lm-evaluation-harness) and tokens/s with your kernels. Find the most sensitive layers and propose a mixed-precision recipe.
deliverables: repo with emulators, quantizers, kernels and an eval harness
README with accuracy-vs-bytes Pareto plot and per-layer sensitivity heatmap
a 600–1200 word write-up of findings and the recommended recipe

rubric.solid: At least 6 configurations evaluated on both metrics with measured speed; scripts reproduce every number
rubric.exceptional: A mixed-precision recipe that beats uniform int4 or MXFP4 on both perplexity and bytes per parameter, with kernel speedups measured

title: Accelerator architecture: systolic arrays, TPUs, dataflows
why: A compiler for a TPU-like accelerator needs a model of the hardware: dataflow, buffer sizes and array utilization. This module builds that model and a backend for it.

steps.title: In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a Tensor Processing Unit (ISCA 2017)
steps.detail: The systolic matrix unit, the roofline comparison with CPU and GPU, and why response-time limits shaped the design.

steps.title: TPU v4: An Optically Reconfigurable Supercomputer for Machine Learning with Hardware Support for Embeddings (ISCA 2023)
steps.detail: Optical circuit switches and SparseCores; list what changed since TPUv1.

steps.title: Efficient Processing of DNNs: A Tutorial and Survey (Sze et al.)
steps.detail: Section V.B, energy-efficient dataflows: weight-stationary, output-stationary, no-local-reuse and row-stationary.

steps.title: Eyeriss: An Energy-Efficient Reconfigurable Accelerator for Deep CNNs (JSSC 2017)
steps.detail: Row-stationary dataflow and energy cost per memory level.

steps.title: MIT 6.5930/1 Hardware Architecture for Deep Learning (Sze, Emer)
steps.detail: Public course page with syllabus and reading list; lectures and labs are on MIT Canvas. Use the reading list to choose papers on dataflow and mapping.

steps.title: Timeloop/Accelergy
steps.detail: Follow the Tutorials & Examples on the site; map a conv and a matmul onto a modeled accelerator and compare mappings by energy and cycles.

steps.title: Gemmini (Berkeley)
steps.detail: Read the README Architecture section: an open systolic-array generator with an ISA and software stack.

steps.title: Cycle-level systolic array simulator
steps.detail: Python or C++: NxN PEs, weight- and output-stationary modes, SRAM buffers, DMA; count cycles and accesses.

steps.title: Compiler backend for your simulator
steps.detail: Lower your compiler's matmul/conv to tiled instructions for the simulator; pick tile sizes by buffer capacity.

build: A cycle-level systolic array simulator with two dataflows, plus a backend in your compiler that targets it.
check: Simulator matches numpy outputs, and its matmul cycle count is within 5% of your analytic formula including fill and drain
A plot of utilization vs. matrix shape, with the drop for small and skinny matrices explained
Your compiler's tiling beats naive tiling in cycles on a ResNet-50 3x3 conv layer
You can explain from the TPU papers why TPUs use large systolic arrays and bf16
outcomes: Estimate accelerator cycles and energy from dataflow, array size and buffer sizes
Write a compiler backend that tiles matmul and conv for a non-GPU target
stuck: Simulator too slow: validate cycle-exact on small cases, then compute per-tile cycles analytically
Cycle counts off: count the (N-1) fill and drain cycles of the systolic wavefront
Mapping space too large: prune by buffer capacity first, as Timeloop's mapper does
Energy numbers arbitrary: use relative per-level access costs from the Sze et al. survey

project.title: Design-space exploration of a transformer accelerator
project.brief: Extend your simulator with a vector unit and a two-level on-chip memory, then sweep array size, buffer size and dataflow for one GPT-2 small transformer layer in prefill (seq 512) and decode (batch 1-16). Use your compiler to generate the mappings and plot cycles, energy and an area proxy (PE count plus SRAM bytes).
deliverables: repo with simulator, compiler backend and sweep scripts
README with Pareto plots and a validation section against analytic models
a 600–1200 word write-up recommending a design for decode-heavy serving

rubric.solid: Validated simulator, at least 50 design points, a clear prefill vs. decode comparison
rubric.exceptional: Results cross-checked against Timeloop on at least 3 design points, plus a quantified finding such as switching dataflow between prefill and decode

title: Distributed training and inference at scale
why: Large models do not fit on one GPU. This module covers how training and serving systems shard models, what communication each scheme adds, and how to measure it.

steps.title: How to Scale Your Model (JAX scaling book)
steps.detail: Part 1 (rooflines), Part 3 (sharded matmuls), Part 4 (transformer math) and Part 5 (training); do the worked problems. Part 12 covers GPUs.

steps.title: The Ultra-Scale Playbook (Hugging Face)
steps.detail: Data, tensor, pipeline, context and expert parallelism, with measured throughput and memory.

steps.title: ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models
steps.detail: Section 3 (where memory goes), Section 5 (optimizer, gradient and parameter partitioning) and Section 7 (communication volume).

steps.title: Getting Started with Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP2)
steps.detail: Run the fully_shard example, then profile how all-gather and reduce-scatter overlap with compute.

steps.title: Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism
steps.detail: Column- and row-parallel MLP and attention; count the all-reduces per layer.

steps.title: Efficient Large-Scale Language Model Training on GPU Clusters Using Megatron-LM
steps.detail: Section 2.2 (pipeline bubbles, 1F1B, interleaved stages) and Section 3 (choosing tensor, pipeline and data parallel sizes). GPipe is arXiv 1811.06965.

steps.title: Ring Attention with Blockwise Transformers for Near-Infinite Context
steps.detail: Blockwise attention across devices with KV blocks passed around a ring, overlapped with compute.

steps.title: GShard: Scaling Giant Models with Conditional Computation and Automatic Sharding
steps.detail: Expert parallelism and all-to-all dispatch; Switch Transformers is arXiv 2101.03961.

steps.title: Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving with PagedAttention (vLLM)
steps.detail: KV-cache paging and continuous batching.

steps.title: NCCL environment variables (NCCL_ALGO, NCCL_PROTO)
steps.detail: The algorithms (Ring, Tree, NVLS, ...) and protocols (LL, LL128, Simple) NCCL chooses from; force each on an all-reduce and measure bandwidth vs. message size.

steps.title: Mini-parallelism library
steps.detail: On torch.distributed: ZeRO-3-style parameter sharding, a 1F1B pipeline and a tensor-parallel MLP; test correctness on 2 processes with gloo, then on 2-8 GPUs.

build: A from-scratch library (FSDP-style sharding, tensor parallelism, 1F1B pipeline) training GPT-2 small (124M) on multiple GPUs, with communication profiled.
check: For each parallelism, the loss over 200 steps matches single-GPU training to within 1% at the same global batch and seed
Measured memory per GPU matches your ZeRO math within 10%
A profiler trace shows all-gather or reduce-scatter overlapped with compute
You report MFU and the pipeline bubble fraction (p-1)/m for each run

Bubble larger than expected: compare microbatches m to stages p; the bubble fraction is (p-1)/m

project.title: Scale a model and publish an MFU report
project.brief: Train a GPT-2-style 1.3B model on 8 GPUs (A100/H100 class) using your library with 2D or 3D parallelism, and push MFU as high as you can with an ablation of each change. Optional: ring attention at 32k context, or expert parallelism for an 8-expert MoE variant.
deliverables: repo with the library, configs and launch scripts
README with MFU, tokens/s and memory tables across parallelism configs plus profiler traces
a 600–1200 word write-up on what limited scaling and how you fixed it

rubric.solid: >=35% MFU on 8 GPUs with loss matching a reference run and an ablation table
rubric.exceptional: >=45% MFU, or a working long-context or MoE extension, with a cost model that predicts measured step time within 15%

title: Research, open source and career
why: Hiring managers and grad committees look for evidence: merged PRs in real compilers, a reproduced paper, leaderboard results and clear writing. This module produces that evidence.

steps.title: Karpathy, A Recipe for Training Neural Networks
steps.detail: Apply its process to reproductions: inspect the data, overfit a small case first, and verify each step before scaling.

steps.title: Simon Peyton Jones, How to Write a Great Research Paper
steps.detail: Seven concrete suggestions; apply them to your reproduction write-up.

steps.title: Pick and reproduce a recent paper
steps.detail: For example KernelBench (linked), a FlashAttention variant or one of the quantization papers from Module 36. Match one headline number, then run ablations.

steps.title: KernelBench
steps.detail: Solve Level 1 (single-kernel operators) and Level 2 (fusion patterns) problems by hand and track speedup over PyTorch; read how the benchmark scores LLM-written kernels.

steps.title: GPU MODE
steps.detail: Community site for the GPU MODE kernel leaderboards and lectures; find a currently open competition.

steps.title: GPU MODE reference kernels
steps.detail: Problem definitions and reference implementations used by the leaderboards; submit a solution to one.

steps.title: Land a PR in tinygrad
steps.detail: Read the README's Contributing section: no code golf, docs and whitespace PRs closed, claimed speedups must be benchmarked, large diffs not reviewed, and PRs that look AI-written from new contributors are closed. Start from a bounty or a bug with a failing test.

steps.title: Or land a PR in PyTorch
steps.detail: Look for 'good first issue' labels in Inductor and Dynamo; follow the CLA and test instructions.

steps.title: Or Triton / vLLM
steps.detail: Small backend fixes or performance issues; vLLM kernels are at github.com/vllm-project/vllm.

steps.title: Portfolio and interview prep
steps.detail: Pin 4-6 project repos. Practice, in 45 minutes each: a tiled matmul, a reduction, roofline math, a fusion pass and a sharding cost estimate.

build: One reproduced paper with a public report, at least one merged PR in a major ML compiler/runtime, a leaderboard submission and a polished portfolio.
check: A merged (not only opened) PR in tinygrad, PyTorch, Triton, vLLM, JAX/XLA or MLIR
Reproduction matches a headline number within the paper's reported variance
A ranked GPU MODE leaderboard submission or a KernelBench result with a write-up
In a timed mock interview you derive roofline numbers and write a correct tiled kernel
outcomes: Reproduce a systems paper's headline result and report where it differs
Get a change reviewed and merged in a large open-source compiler or runtime
stuck: PR stalls: pick issues maintainers asked for, keep diffs small, include benchmarks, reply quickly
Reproduction does not match: check hardware and library versions, then email the authors one precise question
Too many goals: one paper, one PR, one leaderboard entry
Interview nerves: practice out loud with a timer and explain tradeoffs as you code

project.title: Capstone: a research-grade contribution
project.brief: Combine a reproduction with one new result, for example a kernel paper ported to a new GPU generation or precision, or a scheduling result applied to a different compiler, and upstream the useful part. Present it as a short paper and a talk.
deliverables: repo with code, scripts and data to reproduce every figure
README with headline results and links to merged PRs
a 4-6 page workshop-style paper and a 15-minute recorded talk

rubric.solid: Reproduction matches, one merged PR, a paper with clear claims and ablations
rubric.exceptional: Accepted at a workshop (for example an MLSys or NeurIPS workshop), or a merged feature that maintainers build on, plus a talk at GPU MODE or a reading group
